text:
Small weekend victory: the departure display in our shared workshop now works without an internet connection. 🚌

It reads a timetable from a plain text file on a memory card. No account, no dashboard, no mysterious cloud service. If the card is missing, it shows “check the printed timetable” rather than yesterday's departures.

Reply: “Does it know about cancelled buses?”
No, and that limitation is printed under the screen. This is a convenient clock with a timetable, not live travel information. I would rather make that boring distinction obvious than have someone miss the last bus.

The hardest part was making the display readable from a chair on the other side of the room. My first version had enormous icons and tiny numbers. The second has no icons at all.

I'll put the wiring notes up after another week of testing. For now the whole thing is held together with a very undignified strip of purple tape. #SmallProjects

I thought the little utility I wrote for naming scanned photographs was finished. Then someone tried a folder containing three pictures with exactly the same date.

The program had been very confident about a situation I had never tested. 😬

Today's change is not clever: show the proposed names first, refuse to overwrite anything, and let the person choose a suffix. A dry run should be useful enough that you actually want to look at it.

“Why not sort by the camera metadata?”
Because these are photographs of photographs. The camera dates describe the afternoon we borrowed the scanner, not the summer in the pictures.

Also discovered that people remember a garden shed much more reliably than they remember a year. I'm adding a free-text note, separate from the filename. Sometimes the information worth preserving isn't the information that fits neatly in a date field.

No face recognition planned. We can ask the people who know these pictures while they're sitting right here.

The bicycle basket rattled for a month. I finally tightened one small nut and the entire journey sounded different. 🔧

Naturally, I celebrated by taking the long way home and discovering a completely unrelated squeak.

A neighbour lent me the right-sized spanner instead of letting me use pliers again. There is a lesson here about having fewer tools but knowing which ones you need. There is also a lesson about returning borrowed tools before they become permanent residents of your kitchen.

For anyone asking about the basket liner: it's an old shopping bag, folded twice. I can remove it when it rains, and small things no longer escape through the holes.

I didn't take a before-and-after video. The before sound would have been mostly wind, and the after would have been me announcing that I had become a professional mechanic.

Next job is checking the lights. Not every improvement has to come with a new purchase. #EverydayRepairs

Made a large-print keyboard map for the computer at the community desk. The shortcuts haven't changed; the way we explain them has.

Instead of a dense sheet beside the monitor, there are now three cards: writing, finding things, and asking for help. Each has an example you can try without risking an existing document.

One visitor pointed out that “press the key on the left” wasn't helpful when the keyboard was slightly turned. Naming the key and showing its shape worked better.

Another asked whether closing a window deleted their work. That question deserves a clear answer, not a hurried demonstration followed by “it's easy.”

We're keeping the cards editable. The first person to use them found two mistakes, which is exactly why they were printed on cheap paper rather than laminated immediately.

Tiny interface changes, many cups of tea. ☕ If you've made instructions for a shared computer, what did you learn only after watching someone use them?

Cooked enough lentil soup for three lunches, then realised the containers were all different sizes. This is why “one portion” is not a useful unit in my kitchen.

I filled them by weight this time. The smallest container still looks more satisfying because it's full to the top. Apparently my eyes have their own accounting system.

Recipe notes, before I forget: toasted cumin, chopped carrots, red lentils, water, and lemon at the end. I tasted before adding salt because the leftover vegetables were already seasoned. No impressive equipment involved.

Reply: “Can you freeze it?”
I usually do, after cooling and dividing it. Leave room in the container, label it, and don't expect yourself to identify an anonymous orange block several weeks later.

The nicest part was taking one portion to a friend who had spent the morning assembling shelves. They provided bread and a detailed account of which screws were left over. Excellent lunch conversation. 🥣

Tried using my old laptop with the touchpad disabled for a morning. Not as a productivity challenge; I wanted to find the places where our club's website trapped keyboard focus.

The answer was: more places than I expected.

The photo carousel was particularly ambitious. It wanted the arrow keys, the page wanted the arrow keys, and I mostly wanted to leave.

I've replaced the carousel with ordinary links to a gallery. The page is less animated and much easier to navigate. A friend using magnification also prefers it because the pictures stop moving away while being inspected.

Different people need different ways in. A simple site can still exclude people if we test it only in our favourite way.

There are two remaining problems listed in the issue tracker. Screenshots helped, but a description of the key sequence was what let me reproduce the second one. #Accessibility

Today's workshop experiment: a lamp shade made from folded paper, with a cool-running battery light underneath.

The first fold pattern looked magnificent on the table and blocked nearly all the light when assembled. Strong architectural statement; useless reading lamp.

A narrower strip worked better. The shadows are uneven, which I like, although the photograph makes them look much sharper than they are in the room.

Someone suggested drawing the pattern on a computer. I might, eventually. Right now folding scrap paper is faster than deciding where to put the first point in a drawing application.

I'm making a note of the failures as well as the dimensions. “Use thinner paper” is more useful to future me than a lovely picture with no explanation.

The prototype is staying on my desk while I work on a less wobbly base. 💡

We opened the seed-swap drawer today and found six envelopes labelled only “the tall ones.” 🌾

I admire the confidence. Unfortunately, tall is a category shared by rather a lot of plants.

The new labels have room for the plant name, the year collected, and whether the identification is certain. Unknown seeds aren't going into the swap box. A question mark is useful information; it shouldn't disappear when handwriting gets copied onto a neat label.

A volunteer brought photographs of the parent plants, which helped with two envelopes. The others are being returned to their owners for clarification.

Best conversation of the afternoon: a child asked why seeds from one flower didn't all look identical. We ended up with three drawings, a magnifying glass, and more questions than we started with.

The drawer itself is just a rescued filing cabinet. We're spending our effort on the information inside it before we paint anything a fashionable colour. #CommunityGarden

The museum's little listening station has a new “start again” button. It is physically larger than the button we originally bought, because visitors were pressing the speaker grille instead.

That was not user error. The grille looked like a button and the actual button looked like a screw.

We also moved the instructions from above the screen to beside the handrail. People were already looking there while deciding where to stand.

The recording plays locally, so a network outage doesn't turn an exhibit into an apology. A printed transcript remains available even when everything is working.

I'm sharing the enclosure drawing later this week, once I remove measurements that only make sense in our particular cabinet. A reusable plan shouldn't require someone to own exactly the same accidental piece of furniture.

Thanks to the volunteers who tested it while wearing gloves. That single suggestion found a problem I had missed through an entire afternoon of careful bare-handed testing. 🎧

Learning a drum pattern very slowly has revealed that I do not, in fact, know where my left foot is. 🥁

Hands: reasonably confident.
Right foot: enthusiastic.
Left foot: apparently attending a different rehearsal.

The teacher asked me to tap the rhythm on my knees before touching the kit. It felt childish for about ten seconds, then suddenly made the missing beat obvious.

At home I'm using a practice pad and counting aloud. The point isn't to be quiet enough that nobody notices; it's to agree on a reasonable practice time with the people sharing the building.

Today's recording has one clean bar near the middle. I saved the whole take so I can hear how I arrived there, rather than cutting out a tiny success and pretending it happened on demand.

If you play an instrument, do you keep early recordings? I find them embarrassing until enough time has passed for them to become encouraging. #LearningInPublic

A reminder from today's photo-sorting session: cropping a picture doesn't necessarily remove the location information stored with it. 📷

We checked the exported copy, not just the original, before posting images from the youth club's outing. The aim wasn't to make the children invisible; it was to avoid publishing details nobody had agreed to share.

Faces, name badges and the noticeboard behind the group needed a look too. A beautifully blurred face doesn't help much if a full name is sharp in the background.

Reply: “Isn't this a lot of effort for a harmless photo?”
It took a few minutes because we had decided who would check it. The difficult version is discovering the problem after everyone has reshared the image.

Our checklist is deliberately short. If it becomes a document people only pretend to read, it has failed.

The final picture is mostly muddy boots and a very large puddle. It tells the story perfectly well. #PrivacyByPractice

We ran a practice session on suspicious messages at the repair café. No surprise tests, no public leaderboard, and nobody was labelled “the person who clicked.”

Participants knew the messages were examples. They still found useful questions to ask: Was I expecting this? Can I check through a route I already trust? Why does the message want me to hurry?

The most convincing example wasn't full of spelling mistakes. It was a polite, ordinary-looking request that happened to arrive during a busy afternoon.

Someone said they would ask a colleague before opening it. That is a sensible control, not a sign that training failed.

We used invented organisations and addresses ending in .example. Nothing in the handout led to a live login page.

Next session will spend less time spotting tiny visual clues and more time on what to do when you're unsure. A reporting route that answers kindly is part of the system. 🔎 #SecurityCulture

The password-reset instructions at our lending library used to end with “contact support.” Support was, in practice, a volunteer who was only there on Saturdays.

We have now written down what happens on Tuesday.

This sounds like an administrative improvement rather than a security improvement, but the old gap encouraged people to share one working account while waiting for help.

The new process doesn't ask volunteers to invent exceptions at the desk. It explains what they can verify, what they cannot, and when an account must wait for the designated person.

“Could you automate all of it?”
Possibly, but that isn't the first problem to solve. We need a process that works when the usual person is away and doesn't depend on recognising someone's face.

The public instructions are short. The private checklist has the operational details and a date for the next review.

Today's small win: nobody has to guess which mailbox is being watched. 📚

Our neighbourhood association asked everyone to enter a date of birth on the membership form. I asked what we used it for.

After a surprisingly long conversation, the answer was “we think it was on the old form.”

We removed the field. For the one activity with an age restriction, the organiser will collect only the information needed for that activity, at the point it is needed.

This isn't a claim that collecting less information magically solves every problem. It does mean there is less information for volunteers to lose, copy into another spreadsheet, or retain indefinitely because nobody knows who may delete it.

A member also asked for a paper option. That should not require a special explanation or an embarrassed conversation at the desk.

We're listing the purpose next to each remaining field. If we can't explain it in an ordinary sentence, we probably haven't finished deciding whether to ask the question. #DataMinimisation

Preparing an old tablet for reuse and discovered that “remove the app” was not the same as “remove the account.” A useful thing to learn before handing it to someone else.

I'm following the manufacturer's reset instructions and checking the result. The original owner is doing the account steps themselves; I don't need their password to be helpful.

A clean-looking home screen isn't proof of a clean device. Equally, I don't want to promise a level of data recovery protection that I haven't actually checked.

For our donation scheme, devices with uncertain reset status are separated from devices ready to distribute. The labels describe the state, not just whether the hardware powers on.

The new recipient will get a short setup sheet and the charger that actually fits. 🔌

If you're organising something similar, decide who handles the account-transfer questions before a table full of enthusiastic volunteers starts inventing answers. #ReuseSafely

Tried a sign-in method that doesn't involve typing a password into the shared office tablet. The nicest part was not the clever technology; it was explaining how to get back in after losing a device.

We tested recovery with a spare account, while everyone was calm and nobody had a meeting starting in two minutes.

One instruction referred to an old menu label. Another assumed the person still had access to the same email address. Both were easy to miss when reading the guide at my own desk.

Reply: “So which method should everyone use?”
I'm not making that recommendation from one afternoon's test. Different accounts, devices and recovery arrangements have different requirements.

What I can recommend is treating recovery as part of setup rather than a future problem. Store the appropriate recovery information somewhere deliberate, and check that the person who needs it knows where it is.

Smooth sign-in is good. Recoverable sign-in matters too. 🔐

A gardening app asked for permission to read my entire contact list before I could record a tomato plant.

The tomato has not yet expressed an interest in networking. 🍅

Joking aside, I declined and checked whether the basic function still worked. It did. That made the explanation on the permission screen especially confusing: “required for a better experience” did not tell me what was required for which feature.

I sent a short, specific report rather than a screenshot containing my contacts. The developer replied that the request belonged to an optional sharing feature and had been shown too early.

A later update moved it to the point where you invite another person. That is a much more understandable moment to make a choice.

This was a small application with a responsive maintainer, not evidence that every permission request is malicious. Still worth asking whether the information requested matches the task you're trying to perform. #Privacy

Walked past a conference registration screen that displayed the previous visitor's details while waiting for the next person.

I quietly told the organiser. They switched it to a blank confirmation page and checked the rest of the desks.

No dramatic social post, no photograph of the person's information, no attempt to see how much else the system might reveal. You can report a problem without turning the report into another disclosure.

What I liked was the response: “Thank you, we'll fix that now.” Nobody asked why I had noticed or suggested that looking at a public screen was suspicious.

The team later added a reminder to their setup checklist: test what the screen shows before, during and after a registration, including when someone walks away halfway through.

A surprisingly large part of privacy is what remains on a screen when the task appears to be over. Good catch by the next volunteer too: the confirmation printer had a similar issue. 🖨️

We practised our small organisation's incident phone tree today. The scenario was an unavailable booking calendar, not a Hollywood hacker taking over the building.

First discovery: one contact number belonged to a phone that stays in a locked cupboard.
Second discovery: two people thought the other person was responsible for the customer notice.
Third discovery: the paper copy was much easier to find than the shared document, because the exercise assumed our normal accounts were unavailable.

Nobody touched the live service. We talked through actions, wrote down decisions, and marked the places where the instructions were missing.

The useful output was four changes to a checklist, not a score for who responded fastest.

I'm glad we kept the exercise modest. It gave new volunteers room to ask basic questions without an audience waiting for a perfect answer.

Next review: confirm that the revised contact list actually reaches the people named on it. A tidy document is not the same thing as a working plan. ☎️

Drafting a notice about a service interruption and trying very hard not to write “no evidence of a problem” when what we mean is “we haven't finished checking.”

Those sentences can sound similar in a hurried update. They make very different promises.

The current draft separates what users can do now, what we know, what remains uncertain, and when we'll update the page again. It also gives a route for urgent requests that doesn't depend on the interrupted service.

A colleague crossed out three reassuring adjectives and added one useful time. Much better editing than another paragraph of corporate sympathy.

We are not publishing names or raw logs in the public notice. The people investigating still have access to the evidence they need.

Writing the draft exposed several real gaps in our communication plan.

Plain language doesn't remove uncertainty. It can at least keep us from hiding it. #IncidentComms

Ask: What household object became less useful when it gained a screen?

My vote is the washing machine. The old dial showed the selected cycle from across the room. The new display tells me everything except what the machine will remember after a power cut.

Reply: I disagree about screens in general. Our oven's clear text labels are much easier for my father than the worn symbols on the old one. The problem sounds like hidden state, not pixels.

Reply: Physical controls have hidden state too. Try a timer that resets when you turn it past zero.

Original poster: Fair correction. What I miss is being able to inspect the state without waking the interface. I don't particularly care whether the information is printed, lit or mechanical.

Reply: Repairability belongs in this conversation. A broken display can disable controls that still work perfectly well underneath it.

Good discussion. I came for complaints about appliances and left thinking about what “off” means.

Show: I made a searchable catalogue for the tools in our shared shed.

Before anyone asks, yes, a spreadsheet would have worked. The project began as an excuse to learn a database, and only later became something other people wanted to use.

Each tool has a photograph, a shelf location, and the date someone last checked it. We aren't tracking individual borrowers in the public view.

Reply: How do you handle the tool being put back in the wrong place?

Not very elegantly yet. “Shelf location” means where it should be, not a promise that it's there. The page now says that explicitly, after a volunteer spent twenty minutes trusting it too much.

Reply: A label on the shelf might deliver more value than another search feature.

Agreed. We printed those first this weekend. I still enjoyed building the search, but the shelf labels solved a problem the search could only describe.

The code is small. Keeping the catalogue accurate is the actual ongoing work.

> A paper map never runs out of battery.

True, but it can be out of date, difficult to read in poor light, and soaked through by lunchtime. I'd rather teach several ways to navigate than make this a contest between virtuous paper and foolish electronics.

Reply: On a long walk I carry both. The phone is convenient; the map helps me understand the area rather than following one instruction at a time.

Reply: The useful backup is the one you know how to use. A compass kept in its packaging is mostly decorative.

Reply: Also tell someone your route and expected return. That's a different kind of redundancy.

Original commenter: This is the point I was trying to reach. Reliability isn't a property of one object in isolation. It depends on the route, the weather, the person using it, and what happens when the first plan stops working.

I would happily read more ordinary failure stories and fewer arguments about which device proves you're an authentic walker.

Ask: When does a personal script need documentation?

I wrote a file converter six years ago, forgot the assumptions, and spent this morning proving that its most confusing behaviour was something I had deliberately requested.

Reply: The moment it produces an output you would be annoyed to lose. Document what it reads, what it writes, and whether running it twice changes anything.

Reply: For me the important note is “why this exists.” The code usually tells me how; it rarely tells me which alternative caused enough trouble that I wrote the script.

Reply: A sample input and expected output have rescued more of my projects than long installation guides.

Original poster: I added those, plus a warning that the converter does not preserve comments. That omission was obvious when all the files were mine. It would be a nasty surprise for somebody else.

No new features today. Just enough explanation that future me won't have to conduct another archaeological investigation.

A local cinema is testing quiet booking hours for people who prefer to buy tickets without background music or promotional screens changing constantly.

I'm interested in the idea, but the announcement doesn't say whether the lighting changes too. That detail may matter more than the word “quiet.”

Reply: Ask them to describe the conditions rather than assigning a label. What sounds relaxing to one person may be uncomfortable to another.

Reply: And make sure the information is available without calling. Some people specifically need to avoid a phone conversation to plan a visit.

Reply: Please include what stays the same. Fire alarms and essential announcements won't be switched off.

Original poster: I sent those suggestions. The manager said the next notice will list the music, lighting and staffing arrangements individually. This is a small pilot, not a claim that one session will suit everyone.

That seems a useful way to start: explain the actual environment, then let people decide whether it works for them.

Show: a tiny local dictionary for the abbreviations in my grandfather's workshop notebooks.

The difficult part hasn't been the handwriting. It's discovering that the same two letters can mean a material on one page and a supplier on another.

Reply: Are you expanding every abbreviation automatically?

No. The original remains visible, and uncertain readings have a question mark. I want the catalogue to make the notebook easier to explore, not silently replace it with my best guess.

Reply: Include photographs of repeated terms. Once a reader learns one person's handwriting, other entries become much easier.

That's on the list. I also added a “same as?” link between two entries without merging them. We may later discover that they refer to different things.

The family contributed several corrections after seeing the first version. One mysterious technical term turned out to be the nickname of a dog that apparently interrupted a lot of work.

Keeping uncertainty visible has made this more collaborative, not less useful.

> Faster checkout is always better for customers.

Only if the person knows what just happened. I used a terminal yesterday that completed the transaction before I understood which delivery option I had selected.

Reply: Speed and clarity aren't opposites. Show the summary at the point where the customer can still change it.

Reply: There are accessibility issues too. A timeout that's generous for one reader can be extremely short for another.

Reply: The shop assistant should be able to explain the state without looking at a completely different interface.

Original commenter: Exactly. I don't want a deliberately slow payment process. I want enough visibility to tell whether I am choosing, confirming or merely watching an animation.

I went back to the shop's feedback form and described the sequence instead of saying “the machine was confusing.” Hopefully that's actionable. The assistant was kind and fixed the order, but a system shouldn't depend on a kind person noticing every misunderstanding.

Ask: What makes a useful error message for a small command-line program?

I'm choosing between a short explanation and printing the entire exception. The latter is helpful to me but probably not to the volunteer importing a list of garden plots.

Reply: Tell them which file or row failed, what was expected, and whether anything was changed. Put technical details somewhere they can include in a report without exposing the whole input.

Reply: Don't suggest deleting a file unless you know exactly what the file contains.

Reply: If the program writes partial output, say so loudly. People will otherwise assume the existence of the output file means success.

Original poster: I changed the default message and added an optional diagnostic mode. The importer now checks the whole input before replacing the previous list.

The best test was asking a friend to fix a deliberately broken example without looking at the source. Watching the first wrong turn was more useful than another hour of arguing about wording.

The school near us lets children borrow simple measuring tools for projects. The kit includes a tape measure, a magnifier, a balance and a notebook of questions rather than experiments to copy.

I like that the questions include “what could make this measurement wrong?”

Reply: Repeating a measurement is surprisingly hard to teach if the equipment always produces a tidy number.

Reply: Let them measure something that changes. A shadow or a growing leaf makes disagreement less embarrassing because there isn't one permanent answer on the back of the card.

Reply: Please distinguish measuring an object from measuring a person. Not every classroom comparison needs to become a ranking of children's bodies.

Original poster: The lending guide does make that distinction. My child's current project is whether the shortest route across the playground is also the route people actually take.

The result so far is a map full of detours around conversations. That may be the most accurate map we've had.

I miss software manuals that explained a task from beginning to end rather than presenting every button as an isolated feature.

Reply: Some of the old manuals were hundreds of pages long and nearly impossible to search. Memory edits out a lot of frustration.

Fair. I don't want the paper or the size back. I want one worked example that begins with a messy real situation and shows what a finished result looks like.

Reply: Then tutorials and reference pages should be separate. A newcomer and an experienced user looking up one option aren't asking the same question.

Reply: The worked example needs to admit its assumptions. Otherwise people follow it successfully and still can't apply the tool to their own case.

Original commenter: That's a better description of what I wanted. I'm revising our association's spreadsheet guide this way: one short end-to-end example, followed by searchable notes. Nobody should have to read a history of spreadsheets to enter next week's room bookings.

What did you make from the vegetables you forgot were in the drawer?

I found a cabbage that was still perfectly usable but clearly losing enthusiasm. Half went into a warm salad with beans; the rest is sliced and ready for tomorrow's noodles. The trick was checking it before buying another one.

Reply: Mine became fritters. Grate, squeeze, mix, and accept that the first one is the cook's snack.

Reply: A reminder to label frozen leftovers with more than “soup.” Future you is not a forensic specialist.

I am absolutely guilty of that. There is currently a container marked “probably squash” in our freezer. It has a date, at least.

No perfect meal plan this week, just trying to notice what we already have. If you're sharing a recipe, please say which ingredients are flexible. Knowing that I can use an ordinary onion instead of a specific variety makes me much more likely to try it. 🥬

Our street's informal walking group tried a shorter route with more benches today. We covered less distance and had a much longer conversation.

One person brought a folding stool, which turned out to be the most popular piece of equipment. Another knew the name of every tree but admitted to getting lost in the shopping centre next door.

For the next walk, we're putting the surface, steps and available toilets in the invitation. “Easy walk” means too many different things to be useful on its own.

Reply: Can people turn back early?
Yes. We'll agree on that before leaving, and nobody will have to justify it. The route is a suggestion, not a test.

Highlight: watching a dog confidently choose a path none of us had considered. We did not follow; it led directly to a closed gate.

If you're starting something similar, a reliable meeting point and a clear finish time seem more useful than a complicated sign-up system. 👟

Found a second-hand puzzle with one piece missing. The seller had drawn the missing shape on the box, which felt much more helpful than a vague “some wear.”

I bought it anyway. The picture is lovely, and the missing piece is in a plain patch of sky rather than somebody's face.

Reply: Make a replacement from cardboard!
That's the plan. I'm not going to pretend it matches perfectly. A tiny cloud in a different blue can become part of the story.

Reply: We used to write the date and the people who finished a puzzle inside the lid. It made lending it more fun.

I like that idea, with permission from whoever joins in. There is room for quite a history under this lid.

Current progress: the edge is done, the cat has inspected the box, and I have discovered that “one more piece” is not a reliable unit of bedtime. 🧩 Photos after I clear the table of everything that isn't puzzle.

The community fridge has a new shelf label: “Please write what it is, when it was prepared, and the ingredients.”

Not just “homemade.” Not just a smiling face. People need enough information to make their own decision about food.

I'm on the cleaning rota this week, so I have also learned that removable labels are a gift to whoever washes the containers. Permanent marker on a mystery lid is less delightful.

Reply: Are there rules about what can be donated?
Yes, and the organiser checks them with the relevant local guidance. The current rules are displayed at the fridge.

A visitor asked where they could leave unopened tea. We added a small separate box for shelf-stable items so they don't get mixed into the chilled shelves.

The project looks simple from outside. Keeping it useful is lots of small, fairly ordinary jobs done consistently. Thanks to the people who do the unphotogenic cleaning. 🧽

My raincoat now has a bright patch over the pocket I caught on a gate. The repair is visible from across the room, which is an improvement on the nearly invisible hole that kept losing my keys.

I practised on scrap fabric first. Very glad I did: the first attempt looked as if a tiny railway had changed its mind halfway through the journey.

Reply: Did you use a waterproof patch?
Yes, one intended for this fabric, following its instructions. A regular decorative patch wouldn't necessarily solve the same problem.

Reply: I always reinforce pockets before they tear.
I admire this level of foresight. I generally wait until the pocket begins distributing my possessions along the pavement.

The repaired coat is going on a wet walk tomorrow. I'll check the inside afterward rather than announcing that it's as good as new on the strength of a dry photograph.

Still, I'm pleased. It looks like mine in a way it didn't when it came out of the shop. ☔

Does anyone else take photographs of library books they decide not to borrow?

Not the pages, just the covers or the catalogue entry. I used to carry home a stack that represented an imaginary week with no work, no cooking and unlimited evenings.

Now I borrow two and keep a list for later. The list is becoming absurdly long, but at least it doesn't need returning on Tuesday.

Reply: My problem is reservations arriving all at once.
Same. Three books about completely different subjects suddenly become a small administrative crisis.

Reply: A “why I wanted this” note helps. Otherwise future me can't remember what the title meant.

That's excellent. Today's note says “maps made by people who walked the route.” I can already see a theme emerging in the things I keep postponing.

The librarian recommended a thin local-history booklet instead of another large volume. It fits in my bag and has already sent me down a street I've never noticed. 📖

The balcony washing line came down in a gust. Nobody was hurt; one towel made a brief attempt at a career in aviation.

I retrieved it from our own courtyard and checked the fixings before hanging anything else. The line looked fine. The tired little bracket was doing all the work.

Reply: Could you attach it to the railing?
I'm asking the building manager rather than guessing. What holds a dry shirt isn't necessarily suitable for a row of wet towels pulling in the wind.

In the meantime, the drying rack has taken over the sitting room. It is an excellent reminder that laundry has several stages and “washed” isn't the same as “finished.”

A neighbour lent us an extra rack and declined my offer of payment in clean tea towels. Apparently the appropriate exchange is helping carry a plant upstairs next weekend.

I like a repair story that ends with somebody borrowing something ordinary. No shopping link required. 🌬️

Our board-game shelf is now organised by how long the rules take to explain, not how impressive the boxes look.

This has exposed a category I had not considered: “short game, surprisingly long explanation.”

Reply: Put player count on the front too. I always choose something perfect for four when five people arrive.
Done. Also marked games where leaving halfway through causes a problem, because people have buses to catch.

Reply: What about cooperative games?
They get a separate small label, not a separate shelf. The goal is to help people choose, not build a classification system that needs its own rules seminar.

Tonight we played a very simple drawing game. The best picture was a lighthouse mistaken for an ambitious salt shaker. Nobody cared who won.

I'm keeping the labels removable. After watching a few sessions, we'll probably discover that the categories we thought mattered aren't the ones visitors actually use. 🎲

First attempt at growing mushrooms from a kit: the instructions said to be patient, and I responded by inspecting it every twenty minutes. 🍄

The box has spent a week looking exactly like a box. Today there are finally little shapes I can point at without imagination doing most of the work.

Reply: Put a photo beside the date so you can see the change.
I have done this. It turns out a photograph taken from the same angle is more informative than ten photographs of me holding the box excitedly.

I keep the supplier's instructions beside the box so I can check each stage as it develops.

My flatmate is mostly relieved that I have found a slow hobby that cannot be improved by buying a faster charger.

Will report back when there's enough to cook, or when the box has taught me another lesson in managing expectations.

We moved the neighbourhood swap table under cover for the wet season. There is now a sign asking people to take home anything still there at the end of the afternoon.

The intention is swapping, not leaving the last volunteer with a pile of unwanted furniture.

Reply: What actually gets taken?
Small kitchen tools, jigsaws and plant pots went quickly today. A very large decorative bowl attracted many compliments and no new owner.

Reply: Please test electrical items before offering them.
The organisers have a separate process for those. The open table isn't accepting untested appliances.

I brought a box of odd buttons, expecting nobody to want them. Two people used them to finish projects that had been waiting for months.

The best part was hearing why a thing was useful to someone else. I spent years thinking the buttons were nearly rubbish. They had simply been in the wrong drawer. 🧵

Small victory: our rehearsal room now has a working clock. Not a connected clock, not a tablet showing a scheduling dashboard. A clock with hands. We finished on time for the first evening in living memory. 🕰️

Reply: Surely the drummer should already have been providing this service?

The drummer would like it recorded that everyone else spent twelve minutes discussing whether the chorus needed to feel more blue.

Also, if you're coming to the open rehearsal on Sunday, the entrance is around the back. The front door belongs to the dentist, who has been remarkably patient about people asking where to put their amplifiers.

Update: someone has offered us a second clock. I fear we are about to introduce distributed systems into a room where we still argue about whose cable is whose. One clock is enough. Please bring your own mug, though; our tea infrastructure remains entirely dependent on individual contributions.

Today's documentation fix was replacing “simply connect the device” with a photograph of the connector. Three people had spent hours trying to use the socket beside it. Both sockets fit. Only one does anything useful. 🙃

Reply: Did you also label the sockets?

Yes! A truly radical deployment of two sticky labels. The photo is there for people reading the guide before the box arrives.

The best part was a colleague asking whether we should apologise for how obvious the new instructions looked. Obvious is the goal. Someone getting this working at a noisy community centre shouldn't have to solve our little industrial design puzzle first.

We also printed a copy because the instructions previously required an internet connection to diagnose an internet connection. Next month we'll test the whole setup with a person who hasn't attended any of the planning meetings. I suspect they will find at least six more things that are obvious only to us.

Bought a second-hand jacket with a spectacular repair inside the lining. Tiny, even stitches in three different colours. Whoever did it clearly wanted the repair to last, but also wanted the next person to enjoy finding it.

I was going to replace the lining. Now I'm making a little patch beside the old one and leaving that work visible. An accidental collaboration across an unknown number of years. 🧵

Reply: Could you post a close-up without the shop label? I'd love to see the stitch pattern.

Done, in the second image. Description: parallel rows of blue stitches around a small brown patch, with one yellow thread tying off the corner. My contribution is the less elegant green square below it.

Please don't be intimidated by the neatness of the original. The jacket was wearable with the hole; it is wearable with my wobbly repair. Clothes aren't an exam. I'm mostly delighted to have found something useful that also contains a small mystery.

A reminder for the neighbourhood history walk: we start at the old water tower, NOT the pub with the same name. Last time we accidentally assembled two separate groups, and the group in the pub understandably seemed reluctant to relocate.

Saturday, 10:30. About forty minutes on level paths, with several places to sit. Free, no booking, and you can leave whenever you need to. The final stop is close to the bus shelter.

Reply: Is it suitable for children?

Yes, but it's a walk with stories rather than a children's activity. There will be photographs of an extremely muddy construction site and an argument about why the station has two front doors. That argument has been going for eighty years; we do not expect to settle it this weekend.

If the weather is awful, I'll post a cancellation here by 09:00. Please don't send anyone's phone number in the replies. You can share the meeting details without sharing personal contact information. ☔

Our team tried silent reading at the start of a planning meeting. Eight minutes to read the proposal, write questions, and drink tea before anybody defended anything.

The surprise wasn't that quieter people contributed more. It was that the confident people changed their minds while reading, before they had publicly committed to the first thing they thought of.

Reply: Doesn't this just make meetings longer?

This one finished fifteen minutes early. We'll try it a few more times before naming a methodology after it.

The useful bit was writing down questions before discussion. We found three different interpretations of “launch”, including one that required a physical launch event and one that meant changing a configuration flag. Better to discover that on page two than on the supposed launch day.

No new software involved. Just an actual proposal sent ahead of time and permission not to talk immediately. A surprisingly difficult feature to ship.

#WorkNotes #Meetings

First attempt at describing my photographs without saying “beautiful”, “stunning”, or “a lovely view”. It turns out those words mostly describe my feelings, not anything someone could use to imagine the picture.

New description: a narrow footbridge crosses a shallow stream; red leaves collect against the upstream rail, and a bicycle leans on the far side. Grey sky. No people visible.

Reply: Do you include the mood at all?

Sometimes, after the concrete details. I'm still learning. For this picture the empty bicycle mattered to the story, while the exact number of railing posts didn't. Someone else might make a different choice.

I also removed the line about the bridge being “abandoned”. I was standing beside it for perhaps ninety seconds. A person could easily have been fetching a sandwich just outside the frame. Photography gives us plenty of opportunities to sound much more certain than we are. 📷

#AltText #Photography #LearningInPublic

Went to a board-game evening expecting to learn one game. Came home having learned that I become intensely competitive about imaginary postal routes.

The rules explanation included “you can cooperate here”, which our table interpreted as an invitation to form a fragile international treaty over a cardboard ferry. The treaty lasted eleven minutes.

Reply: Was it beginner friendly?

Very. The host played a practice round with everyone's cards visible and said we could restart after that. Nobody had to pretend they understood the scoring. That did more for the atmosphere than any icebreaker I've ever encountered.

For next time: bring a snack that doesn't leave orange powder on shared pieces. This is directed mostly at me. Also, if you need a quieter table, mention it when you arrive; there's a small room away from the music. I didn't know that existed until the end, so passing it on here. 🎲

The community radio archive now has thirty years of programme titles in a searchable list. We celebrated by immediately finding three different spellings of the same weekly gardening show. 🌱

This is a catalogue, not a complete audio collection. Some recordings are missing; others can't be published until we sort out permissions. Please don't assume a title without a play button is a broken link.

Reply: Can listeners suggest corrections?

Yes. There's a plain contact link beside each entry. A year, approximate month, or the name you remember is useful. “I think this was the episode about enormous carrots” is also useful, and considerably more entertaining than most catalogue notes.

We're keeping uncertain dates marked as uncertain rather than quietly choosing a plausible Tuesday. It makes the list look less tidy, but it leaves room for someone with an old programme sheet to help us get it right. Thanks to everyone who has already checked a shoebox in the attic.

I gave a talk today with one blank slide on purpose. It said, in the speaker notes, “stop and ask whether the diagram made sense”. Past me knows present me will otherwise continue talking until someone physically removes the clicker.

A person asked the question I'd been hoping nobody would ask. It exposed an assumption in the diagram, and we spent the remaining time fixing it together. Much better than reaching my carefully polished final slide.

Reply: Are you publishing the deck?

Yes, once I've added that correction and written descriptions for the diagrams. The slides alone would currently suggest that a roomful of people applauded an empty rectangle for four minutes.

For anyone preparing their first talk: you can say “I don't know”. You can also say “I drew that badly”. Neither sentence opens a trapdoor beneath the stage. I tested both extensively this afternoon and remain above ground. 🎤

#PublicSpeaking #Learning

Weekend plan: take the slow train to the end of the line, have lunch, come back. No list of attractions. No attempt to turn a free afternoon into a performance review for the town we visit.

Reply: What if there's nothing there?

There is allegedly a bakery and a bench facing the river. These are strong foundations for an afternoon.

Update from the bench: bakery excellent, river moving in the expected direction, one dog extremely interested in our paper bag. We missed the return train because we were watching a delivery boat reverse. This improved the trip by adding time for a second cup of tea.

I'm not proposing a philosophy of travel. Sometimes you need to get somewhere quickly, and sometimes a delayed train is a serious problem. Today we had nowhere urgent to be, and remembering that was the nicest part. Photos later, if any of the boat pictures aren't mostly my thumb. 🚆
